item.research_question: How does the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy change under reciprocating wear conditions at elevated temperatures, and what are the underlying mechanisms?
item.processing_route: Inert gas atomisation using argon followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1050 °C for 10 min under 50 MPa compaction pressure, with passive cooling at 150 K/min until 300 °C
item.test_conditions: Reciprocating wear test using an SRV-Tribometer with a force of 26 N, frequency of 40 Hz, amplitude of 0.5 mm, and Al2O3 counter body (10 mm diameter) at temperatures of 22 °C, 500 °C, 650 °C, 800 °C, and 900 °C for 900 s
key_findings: The SPS samples achieved a dense microstructure with a microhardness of 750 ± 17 HV0.5.
The atomised powder exhibited a mean particle size (d50) of 20 µm with a range of -30 +8 µm.
Wear depth initially increased slightly from room temperature to 500 °C, indicating reduced wear resistance.
A distinct reduction in wear depth occurred at 800 °C, with the highest wear resistance observed at 900 °C.
The average coefficient of friction (COF) decreased with increasing temperature, reaching a minimum of 0.85 at 900 °C.
XRD analysis of wear tracks at 800 °C and 900 °C confirmed the formation of a spinel phase (structure type MgAl2O4).
The SPS process resulted in a multiphase microstructure comprising two bcc phases (B2 and A2) and a minor tetragonal σ-phase.
item.mechanism: The increase in wear resistance at elevated temperatures is attributed to the formation of a stable, protective oxide film via tribo-oxidation, which protects the underlying metallic material, while the wear mechanism transitions to abrasive wear of the oxides.
item.limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, but notes that the σ-phase formation and its specific influence require further investigation.
item.future_work: Further investigations have to be conducted to determine the wear behaviour under different wear conditions, and the influence of the additional σ-phase has to be investigated in subsequent studies.
quotes: The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions.
The highest wear resistance was proven for the test conducted at the highest temperature of 900 °C.
The decrease in wear depth proves the protection of the underlying material by tribo-oxidation and the formaton of a stable oxide film.
